$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {2}^{x}+5) \\  & =\frac{4}{x}-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {2}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Given the function $y=2{x}^{3}+x-3{log}_{6}⁡x,$ find the instantaneous rate of change at $x=3.$ Do not round the answer.

The instantaneous rate of change at $x=3$ is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To differentiate a logarithm with base $a,$ we use the formula

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({log}_{a}⁡x)=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡a}.
$$

To find the instantaneous rate of change at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}+x-3{log}_{6}⁡x) \\  & =2\cdot 3{x}^{2}+1-3\cdot \frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡6} \\  & =6{x}^{2}+1-\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change at $x=3$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=3} & ={(6{x}^{2}+1-\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡6})|}_{x=3} \\  & =6(3)^{2}+1-\frac{3}{3\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡6} \\  & =55-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given the function $y=-3{log}_{2}⁡x+4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-5,$ the slope of the tangent line at $x=1$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope of the tangent at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-3{log}_{2}⁡x+4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-5) \\  & =-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({log}_{2}⁡x)+4\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-5) \\  & =-3\cdot \frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+4\cdot \frac{1}{x}+0 \\  & =-\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+\frac{4}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(-\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+\frac{4}{x})|}_{x=1} \\  & =-\frac{3}{1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡2}+\frac{4}{1} \\  & =4-\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $y=2x-5\operatorname{ln}⁡x$,  find the slope of the tangent at $x=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the slope of the tangent at a given point, we have to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x-5\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)-5\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =2-5\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =2-\frac{5}{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(2-\frac{5}{x})|}_{x=1} \\  & =2-\frac{5}{1} \\  & =2-5 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Differentiating the Product of a Constant and the Natural Logarithm Function
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The derivative of the natural logarithm is the reciprocal function:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{ \textrm{d} x}\left( \ln x \right)= \dfrac{1}{x}
$$

We apply our formula and get

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}   & = \left(5\ln x\right)'\  
                                                    & = 5 (\ln x)'\
                                                    &=5\cdot \dfrac{1}{x}\
                                                    &= \dfrac{5}{x}.
						  

}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\eqalign{
			f'(x) &= \left(2\ln x+x^2-1\right)'\
			&=2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{x}+2x-0\
			&=\dfrac{2}{x}+2x.

}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                     Differentiating a Logarithmic Function With a General Base
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Here, we apply our formula for the derivative when the base of the logarithm is a number other than $e.$ By doing so, we obtain

$$
\eqalign{
			\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(4\log_3 x\right)\
									 &=4\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\log_3 x\right)\
									 &=4\cdot\dfrac{1}{x \ln 3}\
									&=\dfrac{4}{x \ln 3}.

}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating the Slope of the Tangent Line of a Logarithmic Function at a Point
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $y= \log_4 x + \ln x$,  find the slope of the tangent at $x=1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the slope of the tangent at a given point, we have to find $\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
		&= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left( \log_4 x + \ln x \right)\
		&= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\log_4 x) + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\ln x )\
		&= \dfrac{1}{x\ln 4} + \dfrac{1}{x}.
}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+\frac{1}{x})|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
The derivative of the natural logarithm is the reciprocal function:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{ \textrm{d} x}\left( \ln x \right)= \dfrac{1}{x}
$$

We'll prove this result in a future lesson.

tutorials.name: Differentiating a Logarithmic Function with a General Base
tutorials.problem:
For a general logarithm of base $a,$ the derivative is given by

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{ \textrm{d} x}\left( \log_a x \right)= \dfrac{1}{x\ln a}.
$$

Also, recall that whenever $\log$ is written without a base, we can assume that it represents the base $10.$ So, we have

$$
\log x =  \log_{10} x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(\operatorname{log}⁡x) & =\frac{d}{dx}({log}_{10}⁡x)=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡10}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** To see where this rule comes from, we can use the change-of-base formula as shown below.

$$
\log_a x = \dfrac{\ln x}{\ln a}
$$

Taking the derivative and using the fact that $\ln a$ is a constant, then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({log}_{a}⁡x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡a}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡a}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡a}.\end{aligned}
$$
tutorials.title: Differentiating a Logarithmic Function with a General Base

$$

Also, recall that whenever $\log$ is written without a base, we can assume that it represents the base $10.$ So, we have

$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(\operatorname{log}⁡x) & =\frac{d}{dx}({log}_{10}⁡x)=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡10}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** To see where this rule comes from, we can use the change-of-base formula as shown below.

$$
\log_a x = \dfrac{\ln x}{\ln a}
$$

Taking the derivative and using the fact that $\ln a$ is a constant, then, we have

$$

$$
